identification.summary: Cyber Toufan (also written Cyber Toufan Al-Aqsa) is a hacktivist-branded group that emerged in November 2023 and has primarily targeted Israeli organizations with hack-and-leak and destructive (wiping) operations [S1][S4]. Press reporting says it claimed more than 100 victims [S1][S4]. Check Point researchers, quoted in press, called it an Iranian threat actor, while the group presents itself as independent [S1][S4].
identification.firstObserved: 2023-11 (Dark Reading reports the Signature-IT hosting compromise on 16 November 2023) [S1][S4].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name is known to this research pass; none is asserted. Do not merge with Handala or CyberAv3ngers: Check Point is quoted as listing CyberAv3ngers and Cyber Toufan as separate Iran-affiliated groups [S1]. The source dates below are approximate (see gaps).

attribution.confidence: Disputed and unconfirmed. Check Point is quoted by Dark Reading as calling the group an Iranian threat actor [S1]. A threat-intelligence executive quoted by SAN said its patterns, timing and focus mirror Iranian state-aligned activity, while SAN notes the evidence does not conclusively establish state ties [S4]. Other firms were more hedged and the group has not stated its origin [S1][S3].
attribution.basis: Vendor and expert assessments of targeting, timing and operational patterns as quoted in press [S1][S4]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.

objectives: Disruption, data exposure and psychological pressure against Israeli public and private organizations, aligned with the Gaza conflict; the group's 2025 defense-sector leaks were stated to follow Israeli actions in Gaza [S1][S4].

regions: International firms doing business in Israel [S1]
targeting.notes: In late 2025 the group leaked data attributed to defense contractor Maya Engineering and said it targeted 17 defense-linked companies [S4][S5]. These are largely the group's own claims and early reporting [S4].

capabilities.summary: The group compromised Signature-IT, an Israeli hosting company, on 16 November 2023, which gave access to dozens of Israeli companies and government bodies and to international firms doing business there [S1]. It wiped servers, leaked data on Telegram, and later ran follow-on email attacks against victims' employees and customers [S1][S4]. Kevin Beaumont called the group well organized and disruptive [S1]. The group claimed destruction of over 1,000 servers, which is unverified [S1]. In the Maya Engineering case it claimed 1.5 years of network access, enabling access to other contractors; this is a claim [S5]. No malware families or exploit details were found in the sources gathered.

campaigns.name: Signature-IT hosting compromise
campaigns.summary: Compromise of Israeli hosting firm Signature-IT gave access to dozens of Israeli companies and government organizations plus international firms. The group denied that all leaks stemmed from it, contrary to Check Point's view [S1].

campaigns.name: Mass hack-and-leak against Israeli organizations
campaigns.summary: More than 100 organizations were hit in about a month, with data leaks and wiping; victims included government bodies and technology vendors. Check Point noted leaks paused during a cease-fire [S1][S6].

campaigns.name: Follow-on email attacks
campaigns.summary: As leaks slowed the group sent follow-on emails to victims' employees and customers [S1].

campaigns.name: Maya Engineering defense-contractor leak
campaigns.summary: The group leaked CCTV footage and technical documents attributed to Maya Engineering, claiming 17 defense-linked targets and 1.5 years of access. Reported dates vary (late October 2025 per SOCRadar and BreachSense listings via search results); claims are unverified [S4][S5].

diamond.adversary: Hacktivist persona assessed by some vendors as Iran-linked; unconfirmed [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: Supply-chain compromise of a hosting provider, data exfiltration and leaking, destructive wiping, follow-on phishing emails [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Telegram channel used to publish leaks [S4]. Other infrastructure not found in sources.
diamond.victim: Israeli government, technology, retail, academic and defense organizations, and foreign firms using Israeli hosting [S1][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Gaza conflict and Israel-Iran tension; leaks timed to events and paused during a cease-fire [S1][S4].
diamond.technology: Reliance on a single hosting/MSP provider created a single point of compromise for many tenants [S1].

gaps: WebFetch could not reach any publisher host in this run, so all content comes from search-result summaries, not full articles; verify each source before use.
Publication dates for S1-S6 were not visible in results and are approximate, inferred from event timing; confirm them.
The Check Point primary report (listed in the existing record as research.checkpoint.com 2023 11th December threat intelligence report) and Kevin Beaumont's original post were not opened.
Initial access method, malware, wiper names and infrastructure are not stated in the sources gathered.
Iranian state sponsorship is not established; no government attribution was found.
Relationship to Handala and other Iran-aligned personas is not established.
Date of the Maya Engineering leak differs across listings (about 30-31 October 2025); the 2025 campaign and victim claims are unverified.
The SecurityWeek source was removed: its URL was not seen in verification searches; the named 2023 victim list and 'one-third unrecovered' detail were dropped.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Third-party hosting and managed IT providers serving Israeli and allied organizations are key cyber terrain; defense contractors are secondary terrain [S1][S5]. STEP 2: A single provider compromise exposed dozens of tenants, and wiping degraded recovery [S1]. STEP 3: Template: provider compromise, data theft, Telegram leak, wiping, then follow-on phishing [S1][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA: continued hack-and-leak and wiping against Israeli entities timed to conflict events. MDCOA: leaks of allied defense-contractor data or supply-chain compromise of a provider serving US or coalition partners. Candidate indicators: new Telegram leak posts naming defense firms, sudden mass wiping at tenants of one hosting provider, and employee-targeted phishing after a leak [S1][S4][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track hacktivist leak channels and third-party provider incidents affecting partner and DIB organizations [S1][S4]. (2) Authorities: attribution is unconfirmed, so avoid treating it as state action in planning documents [S4]. (3) Mission assurance: verify offline backups and provider-dependency mapping for contractors, since wiping left victims struggling to recover [S1]. (4) Coordination: share leaked-data exposure with affected contractors via DC3 and the DIB program, and with partner nation CERTs [S5].

provenance.importedSummary: Cyber Toufan is a threat actor group that has gained prominence for its cyberattacks targeting Israeli organizations. The group's tactics suggest potential nation-state backing, possibly from Iran. They have been involved in hack-and-leak operations, data breaches, and data destruction, impacting over 100 organizations. Cyber Toufan's activities align with geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and their attacks are characterized by a combination of technical breaches and psychological warfare.
